𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐏𝐬𝐲𝐜𝐡𝐨, 𝟐𝟎𝟎𝟎.⁣
⁣
I rented American Psycho (2000) from a video store when I was 12 years old. I had no idea what I was getting into. Maybe the title intrigued me, or the cover. I didn’t fully understand it back then, but it left a lasting impression. Since that first watch, I’ve seen it at least ten more times. And with each viewing, it reveals something new, something unsettling that lingers.⁣
⁣
What starts as a slick film about a successful Wall Street yuppie slowly morphs into a chilling dissection of a man (and a nation) whose mask is slipping. Patrick Bateman is an embodiment of the American dream pushed to grotesque extremes: the wealth, the status, the designer suits… and the hollowness that follows. He’s everything the ‘80s said you should be, and yet he feels nothing. So he feeds his emptiness with increasingly unhinged behavior.⁣
⁣
Christian Bale is simply phenomenal in the lead role. His performance walks a razor-thin line between absurd comedy and genuine horror.  No one else could’ve played this role quite like him. But what also makes the film so gripping is its satirical edge. It skewers the materialism and moral vacancy of its era: obsessions with business cards, table reservations and facial routines. These ridiculous fixations become signposts of a soulless world. And it’s darkly funny. If you let yourself fall into its twisted rhythm. ⁣
⁣
The film’s ambiguity, especially its ending, has frustrated some viewers. But that’s precisely what makes it stick with you. Did Bateman really do all of this? Or was it all in his head? And does it even matter? The line between fantasy and reality is intentionally blurred. This isn’t just about one man. It’s about the sickness of a culture. It’s about how empty men destroy everything around them in a desperate attempt to feel something.

source_details.synopsis: American Psycho is a 2000 horror comedy film directed by Mary Harron, who co-wrote the screenplay with Guinevere Turner. Based on the 1991 novel by Bret Easton Ellis, it stars Christian Bale as Patrick Bateman, a wealthy New York City investment banker who leads a double life as a serial killer. Willem Dafoe, Jared Leto, Josh Lucas, Chloë Sevigny, Samantha Mathis, Cara Seymour, Justin Theroux, Turner, and Reese Witherspoon appear in supporting roles. The film blends psychological horror and black comedy to satirize 1980s yuppie culture and consumerism, exemplified by Bateman. Ellis considered his novel unfilmable; however, producer Edward R.
